questions.q: A query just sits there with no error message. What does this lesson say is the most likely cause?
options: A warehouse problem — it's suspended and starting back up, or queued behind other queries
The SQL syntax is definitely wrong
The table has been permanently deleted
Snowflake's cloud services layer is down
questions.explain: A query with no error that simply doesn't return is almost always a warehouse problem — auto-suspend restart delay or queueing — not a SQL problem.

questions.q: What does a nonzero avg_queued_load from WAREHOUSE_LOAD_HISTORY indicate?
options: Queries were genuinely waiting for warehouse compute to free up, not failing
The warehouse has been permanently deleted
A resource monitor has suspended the account
The role lacks SELECT privileges
questions.explain: avg_queued_load measures real queueing — queries waiting on compute — which points to sizing/scaling as the fix, not query rewriting.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the most common real cause behind an "Insufficient privileges" error?
options: The user is running as the wrong current role for the session, not necessarily a missing GRANT
Snowflake has no role-based security model
The table was moved to a different cloud region
The warehouse is too large
questions.explain: Because a user can hold a role without it being their current session role, checking CURRENT_ROLE() before touching grants often reveals the real issue.

questions.q: A warehouse that worked fine yesterday suddenly won't start today, with no other configuration changes. What should you check?
options: Whether a resource monitor's credit quota fired, suspending the warehouse as designed
Whether the table's primary key was dropped
Whether Power BI's cache expired
Whether the file format was changed from CSV to JSON
questions.explain: A resource monitor hitting its configured credit quota will suspend a warehouse — this is intended behavior, not a bug, and SHOW RESOURCE MONITORS shows quota vs. used credits.

questions.q: What are the two SHOW GRANTS variants used in this lesson, and what does each answer?
options: SHOW GRANTS TO ROLE (what a role can do) and SHOW GRANTS ON TABLE (who has access to a specific object)
SHOW GRANTS TO WAREHOUSE and SHOW GRANTS TO DATABASE, both showing billing information
SHOW GRANTS ON PIPE and SHOW GRANTS ON STREAM, both unrelated to privileges
There is only one SHOW GRANTS command with no variants
questions.explain: SHOW GRANTS TO ROLE lists everything a role currently holds; SHOW GRANTS ON TABLE lists who currently has access to that specific object — together they pinpoint a missing privilege.
